comments.author: deansaxe
comments.body:
Past CFP:

**Stop Counting Factors... Start Describing Authentication Events**
We began deploying multi-factor authentication because passwords provided insufficient security. More factors equals more
security, right? Yes, but we continue to see authentication attacks such as credential stuffing and phishing! The identity industry needs to stop thinking in the quantity of authentication factors, and start thinking about the properties of the authentication event. As we transition into the era of passkeys, it is time to consider how we describe the properties of our authentication event.

In this talk, we’ll demonstrate how identity providers and relying parties can communicate a consistent, composable collection
of authentication properties. To raise the security bar and provide accountability, these properties must communicate not only
about the authentication event, but about the security primitives underlying the event itself. These properties can be used to drive authentication and authorization decisions in standalone and federated environments, enabling clear, consistent application of security controls.

Dean Saxe, Principal Engineer, Office of the CTO, Beyond Identity
Pamela Dingle, Director of Identity Standards, Microsoft

comments.author: deansaxe
comments.body:
**Stop Counting Factors, Part Deux**

Two years ago, we stood on this stage and argued that the identity industry needed to stop counting authentication factors and start reasoning about the properties of the authentication event. The response from the community confirmed we had struck a nerve.

Since then, we have taken that argument from conference stage to standards body. We explored the idea further at IETF121 and OAuth Security Workshop 2025, and have since co-authored an IETF draft to formalize the terminology. We seek to develop a precise, interoperable vocabulary for describing what actually happened during authentication events.

In this talk, we will walk through the terminology the draft defines: what the terms mean, why the distinctions matter, and how identity providers and relying parties can use them today to drive clearer authentication and authorization decisions. 

We are not here to present a finished standard. We are here because standards development requires the identity community's input. If you have deployed passkeys, built policy engines on top of authentication context, or struggled to describe authentication events consistently across federated systems, your experience is directly relevant to this work.

comments.author: pamelatech
comments.body:
Credential Security Properties: Progress Report

Two years ago, Pamela Dingle & Dean Saxe argued that the identity industry needed to stop counting authentication factors and start reasoning about the properties of the authentication event. The response from the community was strong. Since then, their work has moved from conference stage to standards body resulting in an IETF draft formalizing terminology with a goal to develop a precise, interoperable vocabulary for describing what actually happened during authentication events.

In this talk, Dean & Pamela walk through the terminology the draft defines: what the terms mean, why the distinctions matter, and how identity providers and relying parties can use them today to drive clearer authentication and authorization decisions.

Standardization of credential security properties requires the identity community's input. If you have deployed passkeys, built policy engines on top of authentication context, or struggled to describe authentication events consistently across federated systems, your experience is directly relevant to this work.

comments.author: deansaxe
comments.body:
Containment is the "at rest" state (including in motion in a sync fabric).
- Password in a vault is contained (unless I know the password)
- password in my head is uncontained
- TOTP is contained 

Unlock takes an at rest credential and makes it available for use (may be bounded by an unlock persistence)

Boundary focuses on a real-time generation of an assertion dynamically generated at runtime
- SAML assertions are not contained, but the private key used to sign the assertion MAY be contained and MAY be unlocked and MAY have unlock persistence
- the boundary of the SAML assertion is the expected channel where the assertion is shared

pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
Regenerates the template-managed files now that `draft-dingle-sec-credproperties.md` builds and the test scaffold no longer matches `draft-*.md`.

Ran `make update-files` via the upstream `i-d-template-action` Docker image locally — the `Update Generated Files` workflow itself was failing with a 403 on `git push` because the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN lacked write scope. That's fixed in this PR (see workflow updates below) so the next regen can run from the Actions tab directly.

## What changed
- **README.md** — title, link block, and CONTRIBUTING link now reflect `draft-dingle-sec-credproperties`
- **.github/workflows/update.yml** — adds `permissions: contents: write`, bumps `actions/checkout` to v6
- **.github/workflows/ghpages.yml, publish.yml, archive.yml** — equivalent upstream sync
- **Makefile, .github/CODEOWNERS, .gitignore** — resync with upstream template

History is 8 commits (one per file) — that's how `update-files` works. Feel free to squash-merge if you prefer a tidy main.

## Note
PR prepared by Claude on Dean's behalf.

pulls.author: deansaxe
pulls.body:
## Summary

The `Update Editor's Copy` workflow was failing on `main` after the **Update account recovery (#17)** merge. The `lint-whitespace` check in the i-d-template build flagged trailing whitespace:

```
draft-dingle-sec-credproperties.md contains trailing whitespace
  139: Credential Recovery properties describe...
  148: Recovery mechanism describes the processes...
```

Both lines end a paragraph (followed by a blank line), so the trailing two spaces were meaningless. This strips them, matching the rest of the file.

## Verification

- `grep -n ' $' draft-dingle-sec-credproperties.md` now returns no matches.
- Diff is limited to the two flagged lines (2 insertions, 2 deletions).
